source_passage: In some ways she was far more acute than Winston, and far less susceptible to Party propaganda. Once when he happened in some connexion to mention the war against Eurasia, she startled him by saying casually that in her opinion the war was not happening. The rocket bombs which fell daily on London were probably fired by the Government of Oceania itself, ‘just to keep people frightened’. This was an idea that had literally never occurred to him. She also stirred a sort of envy in him by telling him that during the Two Minutes Hate her great difficulty was to avoid bursting out laughing. But she only questioned the teachings of the Party when they in some way touched upon her own life. Often she was ready to accept the official mythology, simply because the difference between truth and falsehood did not seem important to her.
interpretation:
In this passage from a dystopian novel set within George Orwell's "1984," we encounter Julia—a character contrasting with Winston in terms of susceptibility toward Party propaganda—and whose thoughts hint at an underlying skepticism towards governmental control. The scene illustrates how the omnipresent fear perpetuated by totalitarian regimes, symbolized through daily rocket bombings supposedly from Eurasia but actually orchestrated to maintain public terror and compliance ("just to keep people frightened"), influences inhabitants’ perceptions of reality.

Julia's casual dismissal that these attacks are government-motivated contrasts starkly with Winston’s naive belief. Her incredulity regarding the Party doctrines also suggests a subtle defiance, especially as she finds humor even amidst indoctrination during "The Two Minutes Hate," indicating her personal detachment from or resistance to totalitarian control.

Thus, this passage highlights themes of fear-induced obedience versus individual skepticism and freedom under oppressive regimes—central motifs in Orwell's work. It underscores the fragility of perceived reality controlled by authoritarian powers while subtly questioning whether an individual's will can persist against pervasive indoctrination for its own sake when their lives aren't directly threatened or disrupted ("only question[ing] teachings...when they touch upon her life").
